newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan GDP data helps clear way for early election.
newsitem.headline: Japan GDP data helps clear way for early election.

text.p: Pressure for big public spending to keep Japan's recovery on track faded on Friday after the government said the economy was still improving despite a slip backwards in the three months to June.

The easing of one economic worry combined with diffusion of a political dispute between Tokyo and Okinawa over the concentration of U.S. military bases on the southern Japan island looked set to clear the way for early snap elections.
Data released by the Economic Planning Agency (EPA) showed that Japan's giant economy shrank in the three months to June after stunningly strong growth the previous quarter.

Gross domestic product (GDP) -- a key gauge of the economy's health -- fell a real 0.7 percent in the April-June period from the previous quarter. This would translate into a drop of 2.9 percent on an annualised basis.
Finance Minister Wataru Kubo said ahead of the data's release that policy-makers would decide next week if new steps were needed for the current fiscal year to next March 31.

A senior EPA official, however, said he saw no economic rationale for fresh spending. "We don't need to consider additional government spending for the economy following the latest GDP data for April-June," EPA Vice Minister Shinpei Nukaya told a news conference after the data's release.

In the January-March period, real GDP, which measures the country's output of goods and services minus net income from overseas output, grew a revised 2.9 percent quarter-on-quarter or an annualised 12.2 percent.

Some economists are still worried about a slowdown later in the year. And with election fever in the air, many politicians yearn for an extra budget to woo voters long accustomed to a dose of public spending ahead of national polls.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) is already in the unhappy position of having to defend an unpopular rise in a consumption tax to five percent from three percent next April.
Hashimoto is keeping the public guessing over the timing of a Lower House election -- which need not be held until next July -- partly because his coalition partners are not keen to go to the polls.

But Okinawa Governor Masahide Ota said on Friday that he would take steps to renew leases for U.S. military bases on the Japanese southernmost island, ending a bitter standoff with the central government and boosting prospects of an October vote.
The government's chief spokesman told reporters late on Friday that Hashimoto would decide when to dissolve the Lower House after visiting Okinawa next Tuesday.

Economists said some politicians would like to soften up the electorate with fiscal promises, but added that pledges to craft a big extra budget or freeze the consumption tax would worry not only Finance Ministry mandarins concerned with Japan's huge budget deficit, but financial markets as well.

"Promises that will be made will come back to bite both the economy and the politicians," said Russell Jones, chief economist at Lehman Brothers. "The direction of domestic fiscal policy should be towards consolidation, not expansion."
Japan enjoyed budget surpluses until 1992, but the balance has plunged into the red as a five-year slump has forced the issuance of government bonds to finance stimulative packages.
Many business executives, worried about the deficit and cautiously optimistic that the economy will not slip backwards, are opposed to hefty public works spending this time around.
Politicians also appear to be waking up to the problem.

Financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun said on Friday that a growing number of politicians in the LDP especially were backing the notion of drafting new laws to cut the deficit as a way to win votes in the election.
